It feels like just yesterday I was in an intro class learning about simple data structures, but now I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even basics of quantum computing. store.1: I'm a Computer Science major, and I'm in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is really packed, but it's a good kind of busy. I'm finally taking the higher-level courses that seemed so far away when I was a freshman. It's surreal to be at this stage. It feels like just yesterday I was in an intro class learning about simple data structures, but now I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even basics of quantum computing. It's exciting to see how far I've come!
store.2: My favorite class this semester is definitely Advanced Algorithms. I'm a huge fan of theory when it connects directly to real-world problem-solving. For example, how do we optimize pathfinding in large networks, or what's the fastest way to handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity? These kinds of problems are super fascinating to me. In class, we've been diving into everything from dynamic programming approaches to approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems. It really messes with your head sometimes, but in a good, challenging way. Our professor is great; she has a knack for explaining these dizzying concepts in a really intuitive manner. She'll put up a problem on the board—something you'd think is impossible to solve in polynomial time—and then she'll show us a strategy to at least approximate a solution. Every time I leave that class, my brain's buzzing.

store.4: Aside from Advanced Algorithms, I'm taking a Distributed Systems course(CS 2631), which is probably the second hardest. It's a lot of reading, group discussions, and we're working on a major project that simulates a decentralized file storage system. The group project is definitely an adventure. We have to collaborate with folks who have different coding styles and sometimes different ideas of what the final product should look like. But that's also the beauty of it, right? In a real-world setting, you're never working in a vacuum. You have to be able to integrate your code with others' and handle everything from concurrency issues to node failures gracefully. It's nerve-wracking at times—like last week, I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a single misplaced bracket in one of the config files. But once we got that fixed and everything ran smoothly, it was this huge sense of accomplishment.

store.6: I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which counts toward my major if I combine it with certain other classes. To be honest, I've always been a gamer at heart, so this was a must-take. The professor is actually from the industry; he worked on a couple of indie games that got some decent traction. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, how to implement physics, and even a bit of user experience design. It's unbelievably fun because every assignment is super creative. Last time, I had to design a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept, and it was all about balancing the difficulty curve so players wouldn't get frustrated and quit. Getting that design right was tricky, but it was also rewarding to see it come together.

store.8: I also have an Introduction to Quantum Computing class, which I might have regretted signing up for at first, but now I actually enjoy. It sounds cutting-edge, right? Initially, it was intimidating, but the professor's approach is to make it more about conceptual understanding than pure math. Of course, there is math—like linear algebra out the wazoo—but it's interspersed with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not actually building quantum computers or anything, but we're modeling basic algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they theoretically outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing stuff and has made me rethink how I approach problems.

store.10: I'm also taking a Capstone Project course, which is basically the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. My group and I decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. It sounds fancy, but it essentially means reading a firehose of tweets or posts and analyzing them for words that might suggest a disaster or crisis. We're building an interface that city officials or campus security could theoretically use to see real-time alerts. It's definitely pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major: database management, building an API, front-end interface, plus the ML pipeline. Because it's a real, end-to-end solution, we're also learning about project management and how to keep ourselves organized. One person on our team is the designated "Scrum Master," so each week we have sprints, daily stand-ups, all that agile jazz. It's a lot, but if we can pull it off, I'll be super proud.

store.12: I'm also taking a Philosophy of Mind course, which is my last required non-CS elective. I chose it because it ties back into AI in interesting ways. We discuss consciousness, the concept of mind, and how that might apply to artificial intelligence. It's a smaller class, so we do a lot of class discussions, which is a nice change of pace from all the coding in my other classes. Sometimes it's nice to just sit back and analyze abstract ideas. This course also helps me see the bigger picture, like the ethical implications of building AI systems that could one day mimic or simulate human thinking. Two weeks ago, I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could ever truly experience qualia—like the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a huge topic in the philosophy world, and it was such a trip to research. I think bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is important, so I'm grateful for that perspective.

store.20: I'm a fourth-year computer science major with a passion for coding. My hobbies help me stay sane amidst a hectic schedule of classes and projects. I believe taking breaks and exploring outside interests can actually enhance my programming skills by providing a fresh perspective. It's all about finding that balance.
store.21: Sailing is a hobby that brings me a sense of freedom and challenge. I grew up sailing with my dad on tiny sailboats near a marina. Now, in college, I try to keep up with it during breaks by renting a boat from a local sailing club. I love the rush of wind against the sails and the puzzle-like problem-solving involved in navigating choppy waters. It's a great way to clear my mind and escape the stresses of college life.
store.22: I've found that regular gym sessions have been a great way to balance out my sedentary lifestyle as a computer science major. I started with a basic lifting routine in my freshman year, thanks to a friend who taught me proper form and programming techniques. Now, I aim to hit the gym around four times a week. It's not about becoming a bodybuilder, but about seeing incremental improvements and feeling more energetic throughout the day. Working out is also an excellent stress-reliever after long coding sessions, and it enhances my mental clarity, productivity, and sleep quality. It's a win-win!
store.23: Gaming is a hobby that complements my interest in technology. I enjoy both PC and console games, but PC gaming is more convenient for me as a CS major. Lately, I've been fascinated by co-op survival games where I can gather resources, build shelters, and fend off creatures. This genre offers a different kind of problem-solving experience compared to debugging code. I also occasionally participate in fast-paced shooters, which is a social activity and a mental challenge. Gaming allows me to stay connected with friends and provides a strategic and collaborative experience. Additionally, I've experimented with game development using Unity and Unreal Engine, and I hope to explore this further if time allows. It's exciting to bridge the gap between playing games and creating them.
store.24: Reading has been a lifelong passion for me, thanks to my mom's love of literature. She used to introduce me to fantasy and sci-fi novels when I was a kid, and I'd get lost in other worlds for hours. Even with a busy schedule, I try to squeeze in some reading before bed or on weekends. Lately, I've been fascinated by sci-fi novels that explore artificial intelligence. It's a combination of my academic interests and my curiosity about the future. I enjoy imagining how technology might blur the lines between humans and machines. My current favorite AI-themed sci-fi book is 'The Infinity Courts' by Akemi Dawn Bowman. These books not only provide relaxation but also help me explore philosophical questions about the work I'll be doing after graduation, such as the ethical and social implications of emerging technologies.
store.25: I've found that scheduling my hobbies helps me maintain a healthy balance. Every Sunday, I review my week and plan accordingly. If the weather's nice, I'll head to the gym or rent a dinghy at the local lake. Otherwise, I'll plan indoor activities like co-op games or a workout in my apartment's fitness center. Reading is the easiest to fit in – I do 30 minutes before bedtime, which helps me unwind. It's all about finding time for the things that bring me joy and relaxation.
store.26: I enjoy combining my hobbies to create unique experiences. For example, I've had a day where I spent the morning sailing at the lake, then grabbed lunch, and ended the day playing video games with friends. It was fascinating to see how the experience on the water was similar to coordinating movement in an online co-op. In both cases, everyone has a role to play, whether it's manning the sails or leading the in-game strategy. I love how each hobby demands teamwork, attention to detail, and problem-solving. It's great to see how different activities can complement each other in such meaningful ways.
store.27: I believe that if you're passionate about your hobbies, you'll always find a way to incorporate them into your busy schedule. It's not about doing everything at once; it's about finding small moments to enjoy your hobbies. For example, I might not have hours to read, but I can read one chapter. I might not sail every weekend, but once a month works. And even with just 30 minutes to spare, I can squeeze in a quick gaming match. It's all about being intentional with your time and making the most of every moment.
store.28: I've been involved in undergraduate research since the end of my sophomore year, and it's been one of the most eye-opening parts of my college experience. It's given me a glimpse into how knowledge is created in the tech world, and it's pretty cool to be part of that. I didn't initially see myself going down the research route, but one of my professors noticed my ability to bridge technical coding with user experience and suggested I apply for a research assistant position in a data visualization lab. I was hesitant at first, but taking the leap turned out to be a great decision.
store.29: The lab I'm in is an interdisciplinary space where computer scientists partner with scientists from various backgrounds, including astronomy, environmental science, and neuroscience. We work together to make massive amounts of data more comprehensible. In contrast to the small data projects you might encounter in classes, our lab deals with datasets that are tens of terabytes in size. Visualizing such large datasets so that domain experts can quickly extract insights is a significant challenge. One of my main tasks involves creating front-end prototypes that present slices of data in dynamic, interactive dashboards. This requires the use of advanced JavaScript frameworks, custom visualizations using D3.js, and specialized libraries for volumetric rendering if we're dealing with 3D data.
store.30: The first research project I really got into was about visualizing oceanic temperature changes over time for a climate study group. They had these daily temperature readings from buoys all around the Pacific. The raw data was enormous, with tons of files scattered across different servers, each representing a single day's worth of readings at tiny intervals. Our job was to aggregate and present them in a coherent way that could show patterns over months or even years. I dove in headfirst, writing scripts to clean and unify the data, building a pipeline that could handle near real-time updates, and then designing interfaces that let researchers zoom into a particular region or timeframe. Eventually, I co-authored my first paper on this system. I'm not going to lie, I freaked out a bit when I saw my name in an official publication—it felt so surreal, and it's probably one of my proudest moments in college.
store.31: These days, my research has pivoted to something slightly different but still under the umbrella of data visualization: specifically, I'm working on immersive analytics platforms. We're exploring how VR or AR technologies might help scientists get an even more intuitive feel for complex data. Looking at raw numerical data in a spreadsheet is one thing, and 2D visuals like graphs are another step up. However, actually being able to walk around a 3D representation of data in a virtual environment, touch it, rotate it, and highlight subsets might be a game-changer for some fields. It's definitely a leap from just coding up websites. There's a lot of experimentation involved, including plugging in VR headsets, integrating with engines like Unity or Unreal, and figuring out how to efficiently stream data into a 3D environment. It's all super cutting-edge, but that's what makes it fun. Every day, you're forging your own path because there isn't a huge, established best-practice library for VR data visualization just yet.
store.32: Research life is not just about coding away in a quiet corner. It's a lot of reading, especially when you're trying to solve a specific problem. For example, if I'm working on rendering volumetric data in VR and encounter a bug, I need to search for similar solutions in conference proceedings or workshops. It can be overwhelming, but over time, you learn how to efficiently skim through papers, focusing on the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to determine their relevance. Occasionally, when I find something interesting, I'll share it with the rest of the lab, and we'll discuss how we can incorporate that technique into our workflow.
store.33: I also get to interact with a bunch of graduate students, both master's and PhD students. It can be intimidating at first because they're so deeply immersed in their niche fields, but it's also inspiring. There's this one PhD student in our lab who's been developing a machine learning algorithm to do on-the-fly compression of large datasets. He's trying to integrate it with our VR platform, so the idea is that if you're looking at a huge climate dataset, you don't need to have every single point fully loaded at once in VR—a compressed representation might be enough until you zoom in. It's wild, but super practical for real-time performance. Working alongside him means I get to see how advanced theoretical concepts actually get applied. Some of our best brainstorming sessions happen spontaneously, like in the lab break room, sipping coffee and hashing out how we can offload some processing to the GPU.
store.34: We've also done a few poster presentations at smaller symposiums around campus, which was a great experience. It requires boiling down complex research into easy-to-digest visuals and talking points. The first time I presented, I was sweating bullets, but it turned out to be more like a friendly dialogue. People are genuinely interested in what you're doing. There were even a few folks from local startups who showed up, and they had some interesting perspectives on how VR for data visualization could benefit commercial industries, such as marketing analytics or even architecture. It opened my eyes to how research can transition from academia to real-world applications.
store.35: As for publications, I've been lucky enough to be a co-author on two workshop papers and I'm currently working on a larger conference submission. The bigger conference is the IEEE Visualization Conference(commonly known as IEEE VIS), which is a pretty big deal in our area. We're focusing on a user study that compares traditional 2D dashboards with an interactive VR environment. Our hypothesis is that VR immersion helps researchers spot anomalies or trends faster than they would with just a plain old 2D chart. We ran a small set of user trials, like 15 participants, recorded their times, asked them to fill out a UX questionnaire, and all that jazz. Now we're crunching the data to see if there's a statistically significant difference. Writing the paper is a group effort: I'm handling the sections on system architecture and prototype design, someone else is writing about the user study methodology, and our PI(principal investigator) is weaving it all into a cohesive narrative. It's definitely a balancing act, especially since I have my senior coursework and a capstone project to manage.
store.36: Sometimes I get asked if I plan on going to grad school myself. Right now, I'm leaning toward working in the industry for a couple of years—hopefully at a tech company that values R&D or advanced solution building—before deciding if I want to pursue a master's or PhD. The idea of contributing to cutting-edge knowledge is really tempting, especially in areas like data visualization or machine learning. However, I also want to see how these concepts get applied in real product development. One of my mentors in the lab said that sometimes stepping into industry can give you a better perspective on what problems are truly relevant, so that if you do come back for a PhD, you'll have a more practical approach.
store.37: It's not all sunshine and rainbows. Research can be frustrating. You'll spend weeks on an approach that doesn't pan out, or you'll discover your entire idea has already been done—and improved upon—by a group in Europe or somewhere else. That part can feel like a punch in the gut. However, the key is to adapt. We'll read that existing paper, incorporate their findings, either think of a new angle or a new application, and push the boundary. That's the essence of research. You're never truly starting from scratch; you're building on this giant foundation of what others have done. The sense of collaboration—both within our lab and among the global research community—is something I find really special.
store.38: One story that really stands out is when one of our massive servers crashed a few months ago. We had vital data stored there, some of which wasn't fully backed up(I know, rookie mistake, but we learned from it). I remember the scramble that night: a frantic email chain, Zoom calls with the lab manager, everyone trying to see if we could recover the data. We did manage to restore most of it, but that crisis hammered home the importance of data backups. After that fiasco, we set up a better backup system, plus some checks to ensure we never again rely on a single point of failure. It was stressful, but also kind of a bonding experience for the whole lab.
store.39: Another big plus is that research connects me with professors on a more personal level than just being a face in the lecture hall. My PI is super approachable; if I have a question about the direction of my career or even something I'm struggling with in class, I know I can pop into her office and chat. She's been recommending me for different scholarships, events, and networking opportunities. I got to attend a virtual workshop on immersive analytics that was filled with academic experts from all around the world. Getting to see them debate technical details, propose new frameworks, and even gently tease each other over rival theories was fascinating. It was like I was witnessing the frontier of CS knowledge in real time.
store.40: So yeah, that's basically my journey in the research world so far. It's a lot of work, often more chaotic than you'd expect, but also super rewarding. I love the feeling that what I do in the lab might end up shaping the way scientists understand their data five or ten years down the line. Maybe one day the VR and immersive stuff we're trying to pioneer will become standard tools, and I'll be able to look back and say, 'Hey, I was part of that from the beginning.' It's that sense of contributing to something bigger that really keeps me motivated. Whether or not I go to grad school soon, I know this experience has changed how I think about computer science, about innovation, and even about teamwork. I can't imagine my undergrad years without it—it's definitely enriched my whole perspective on what it means to be a computer scientist.
store.41: I'm glad you have a diverse range of hobbies that showcase different aspects of yourself. It's wonderful that you can discuss topics beyond coding, such as reading, sailing, weightlifting, and gaming. These hobbies add variety and excitement to your life. Thank you for sharing your passions with me!
